extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers / creative writers seeking stronger opening sentences
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for crafting effective first sentences in fiction that introduce character, setting, tone, and promise of story. Focuses on techniques, common failures, and revision practice for opening lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce a protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a protagonist — voice, perspective, identity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening sentence should, if possible, introduce a protagonist by establishing voice, perspective, or some aspect of identity. Example cited: 'Call me Ishmael.' (Melville) — voice in three words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell us when and where
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell us when and where the story is happening
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey temporal and spatial context early to orient the reader. Example cited: 'Many years later, as he faced the firing squad…' (García Márquez) — temporal layering; and 'It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.' (Orwell) — signals wrongness in the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set the tone / signal genre
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening line to establish tone (e.g., ironic, ominous, comic) or to signal the story's genre expectations so readers know what to expect. Example cited: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged…' (Austen) — promise of irony and formal tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possess most craft elements of the story as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: It should also possess most craft elements of the story as a whole: distinctive voice, point-of-view, rudimentary plot promise, and some hint of characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong first sentence often previews the wider story's craft: distinctive voice, clear point-of-view, a rudimentary plot promise that suggests stakes or conflict, and at least a hint of characterization. These elements may be compact but should be present or implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create friction / intrigue
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective openings often contain something strange, contradictory, or unexpected — friction that raises an immediate question and draws the reader in. The line should introduce an element of wrongness, contradiction, or unresolved tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish voice
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in first-person, the opening line is the first chance to show who the narrator is — not just what they say, but how they speak. Voice should be distinctive and reveal character through diction, attitude, and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific techniques
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques recommended for strong openings include: contradiction/paradox (opposing ideas close together), sensory immersion (weather, lighting, atmosphere), in medias res (drop into action), provocative declaration (strong thesis-like statements), mystery/question (implicit or explicit), and unusual fact (a detail that demands explanation). Use these as tools to create friction, voice, or intrigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsider the opening after revision
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconsider the opening once the final draft is complete. The right first sentence often only emerges after the rest of the story has revealed itself; be prepared to rewrite the opening late in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common failure modes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid openings that read like a weather report ('It was a quiet morning…'), generic lines, backstory dumps, clichéd 'character waking up / looking in mirror' scenes, or dictionary-style definitions. (The page references 'Weather report only (Leonard's rule)', 'Generic "It was a quiet morning…"', 'Backstory dump', 'Character waking up / looking in mirror', and 'Dictionary definition of a word' as anti-patterns.)
